bill.title: Proposing a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution of the United States.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that prohibits total outlays for any fiscal year from exceeding total receipts for that fiscal year. The amendment also prohibits (1) increases to the federal debt limit, and (2) a bill that increases revenue from becoming law unless the bill has been approved by two-thirds of each chamber of Congress with a roll call vote.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requiring the federal government to spend no more than it collects in revenue each year. It would also prohibit raising the debt ceiling and require a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate for any bill that increases taxes. If ratified by the states, these rules would become part of the Constitution and could not be changed by ordinary legislation.

industries.rationale: A prohibition on raising the debt limit and strict balanced-budget requirements would directly affect Treasury securities markets and federal borrowing operations.
Mandatory spending limits without deficit financing could constrain federal procurement and defense appropriations.
Balanced-budget constraints could affect federal health program spending, including Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements.
Federal infrastructure and public-works spending could be limited by strict revenue-matching requirements.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would propose a constitutional amendment that prohibits total outlays for any fiscal year from exceeding total receipts for that fiscal year.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who pays tax or gets a federal payment.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in federal spending and borrowing. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
